mission.Launch Location: Cape Canaveral Air Force Station, Florida
mission.Mission Objective: Land a rover on Mars and demonstrate a new way to safely land on the Red Planet and deliver the first-ever robotic rover, Sojourner, to the Martian surface.
mission.Scientific Goals: Analyze the Martian atmosphere, climate, geology, and the composition of its rocks and soil.
mission.Mission Results: Returned 2.3 billion bits of information, including more than 16,500 images from the lander and 550 images from the rover, more than 15 chemical analyses of rocks and soil, and extensive data on winds and other weather factors.
mission.Communication Recovery Attempts: Mission managers tried to restore full communications during the following five months
mission.Additional Details: Mars Pathfinder was originally designed as a technology demonstration.
mission.Source Evidence: Mars Pathfinder article, Key Facts, Photojournal note

equipment.Purpose: Deliver an instrumented lander and a free-ranging robotic rover to the Martian surface, and provide engineering data on new technologies.
equipment.How It Works: Directly entered the Martian atmosphere, assisted by a parachute and airbags, and deployed the Sojourner rover via a rear ramp.
equipment.Main Functions: Landed on Mars, carried scientific instruments, returned images and data.
equipment.Deployment Method: Direct entry, parachute, and airbag landing system
equipment.Additional Details: Named the Carl Sagan Memorial Station.
equipment.Source Evidence: Mars Pathfinder Lander, Airbag Landing, Sojourner Rover

equipment.Dimensions: Stood up to its full height of 1 foot (30 centimeters)
equipment.Purpose: Explore the Martian terrain, acquire images, and take chemical, atmospheric, and other measurements.
equipment.How It Works: Rolled down the lander's rear ramp onto the Martian surface.
equipment.Main Functions: Exploration, imaging, chemical and atmospheric measurements
equipment.Deployment Method: Rolled down the lander's rear ramp tilted at 20 degrees
equipment.Additional Details: Named after American civil-rights crusader Sojourner Truth.
equipment.Source Evidence: Mars Pathfinder Lander, Sojourner Rover, ADDITIONAL INFORMATION: MISSION DURATION

equipment.Dimensions: Measuring 19 feet (5.8 meters) in diameter; 17 feet (5 meters) tall and about 17 feet (5 meters) in diameter
equipment.Purpose: Cushion the impact of the spacecraft on the Martian surface.
equipment.How It Works: Composed of four large bags with six smaller, interconnected spheres within each bag. Inflated by an onboard computer about 330 feet (100 meters) above the surface.
equipment.Main Functions: Enveloped and protected the spacecraft, bounced more than 15 times upon landing.
equipment.Deployment Method: Inflated by an onboard computer during descent
equipment.Additional Details: First time this airbag technique had been used.

equipment.Purpose: Slow the descent of the spacecraft through the thin Martian atmosphere.
Provide a path for the rover to roll down from the lander to the Martian surface.
equipment.How It Works: Tilted at 20 degrees from the surface.
equipment.Location: Carl Sagan Memorial Station, Ares Vallis
equipment.Additional Details: Well within the limits of safe deployment.

equipment.Purpose: Monitor the spacecraft's distance from the ground during descent.
equipment.How It Works: Monitored distance to trigger airbag inflation.
equipment.Additional Details: Triggered the inflation of air bags about 330 feet (100 meters) above the surface.

instruments.Function: Determined the elemental composition of rocks and soils.
instruments.Equipment Associated With It: Mars Pathfinder Lander and Sojourner Rover
instruments.Measurements: Elemental composition of rocks and soils
instruments.Scientific Purpose: Geological and compositional analysis of Martian rocks and soils

instruments.Function: Provided images of the surrounding terrain for geological studies, and documented the performance and operating environment for Pathfinder mission technologies.
instruments.Equipment Associated With It: Mars Pathfinder Lander and Sojourner Rover
instruments.Measurements: Images of surrounding terrain (over 16,500 from lander, 550 from rover)
instruments.Source Evidence: Mars Pathfinder Science Instruments, Mars Pathfinder Lander

instruments.Function: Measured the Martian atmosphere during Pathfinder's descent to the surface, and provided meteorological measurements at the lander.
instruments.Measurements: Atmospheric data during descent, winds, pressure, temperature, and other weather factors
instruments.Source Evidence: Mars Pathfinder Science Instruments, Mars Pathfinder Lander

discoveries.Discovery Name: Ancient liquid water and warm past
discoveries.Description: Findings suggest that Mars was at one time in its past warm and wet, with liquid water stable.
discoveries.Scientific Importance: Indicates past climatic conditions on Mars were capable of supporting liquid water.
discoveries.Related Equipment: Mars Pathfinder Lander and Sojourner Rover scientific instruments
discoveries.Scientific Evidence: Investigations carried out by scientific instruments on both the lander and the rover
discoveries.Source Evidence: Mars Pathfinder Lander, Mars Pathfinder Science Highlights

discoveries.Description: Rounded pebbles and cobbles at the landing site suggested conglomerates formed in running water during a warmer past.
discoveries.Scientific Importance: Indicates the presence of sustained running water in Mars' history.
discoveries.Scientific Evidence: Surface observations and rounded pebbles and cobbles

discoveries.Description: Radio tracking provided a precise measure of the lander's location and Mars' pole of rotation, suggesting the radius of the planet's central metallic core is greater than 800 miles (1,300 kilometers) but less than roughly 1,250 miles (2,000 kilometers).
discoveries.Scientific Importance: Provides constraints on the internal structure and size of Mars' core.

discoveries.Description: Airborne dust is magnetic, and its characteristics suggest the magnetic mineral is maghemite, a very magnetic form of iron oxide.
discoveries.Scientific Importance: Identifies the composition and magnetic properties of Martian airborne dust.

discoveries.Description: Dust devils were seen and frequently measured by temperature, and sensors for wind and pressure. Observations suggested that these gusts are a mechanism for mixing dust into the atmosphere.
discoveries.Scientific Importance: Explains the mechanism for mixing dust into the Martian atmosphere.
discoveries.Scientific Evidence: Measurements by temperature, wind, and pressure sensors

discoveries.Description: Early morning water ice clouds were seen in the lower atmosphere.
discoveries.Scientific Importance: Provides insight into atmospheric water vapor and cloud formation.
discoveries.Scientific Evidence: Visual observations of the lower atmosphere

discoveries.Description: Abrupt temperature fluctuations were recorded in the morning, suggesting that the atmosphere is warmed by the planet's surface, with heat convected upward in small eddies.
discoveries.Scientific Importance: Reveals thermal interaction between the Martian surface and lower atmosphere.
discoveries.Scientific Evidence: Recorded temperature fluctuations in the morning

landing_site.Latitude: 19.17 degrees N (USGS reference frame); 19.30 degrees N (Inertial space)
landing_site.Longitude: 33.21 degrees W (USGS reference frame); 33.52 degrees W (Inertial space)
landing_site.Coordinate Reference Frame: USGS reference frame and Inertial space
landing_site.Inertial Coordinate Method: Two-way ranging and Doppler tracking of the lander
landing_site.Geological Features: North Knob, Southeast Knob, Far Knob, Twin Peaks, Big Crater, Little Crater, Rimshot Crater
landing_site.Horizon Features: Very distant features to the south and east in view; relatively nearby features to the north partially or completely obscured; only the tip of North Knob projects above the local horizon.
landing_site.Nearby Craters: Big Crater, Little Crater, Rimshot Crater, 300-meter crater
landing_site.Surface Description: An ancient flood plain in Mars' northern hemisphere, known as among the rockiest parts of the planet, containing a wide variety of rocks deposited during a catastrophic flood.
landing_site.Terrain Characteristics: Southeast-facing flank of a low ridge; rockiest parts of the planet
landing_site.Distance Measurements: 1.2 km to the northeast (300-meter crater); 5 km scale bar; six-tenths of a mile (1 kilometer) from the point of initial impact
landing_site.Visibility Conditions: Very distant features to the south and east in view; nearby features to the north partially or completely obscured
landing_site.Image Description: Mosaic of Viking orbiter images illustrating the location of the lander with respect to surface features.
landing_site.Source Evidence: Landing Site: Ares Vallis, ADDITIONAL INFORMATION: LANDING COORDINATES, Airbag Landing

mission_timeline.Related Equipment: Delta II 7925 rocket, Mars Pathfinder spacecraft
mission_timeline.Event Description: Mars Pathfinder launched successfully from Cape Canaveral Air Force Station, Florida.

mission_timeline.Related Equipment: Mars Pathfinder Lander, Parachute, Airbag Landing System
mission_timeline.Event Description: Spacecraft directly entered the Martian atmosphere, slowed by a parachute, cushioned by airbags, bouncing ~15 times before coming to rest at Ares Vallis.

mission_timeline.Event Time: Late in the second Martian day (sol 2, night)
mission_timeline.Related Equipment: Mars Pathfinder Lander, Sojourner Rover, Rear Ramp
mission_timeline.Event Description: Sojourner stood up to its full height and rolled down the lander's rear ramp onto the Martian surface.
Sojourner spent 83 days exploring the Martian terrain, acquiring images, and taking measurements.
Final data transmission received from Pathfinder.
mission_timeline.Source Evidence: Key Facts, ADDITIONAL INFORMATION: MISSION DURATION

mission_timeline.Event Description: Mission managers tried to restore full communications during the following five months.
The successful mission was officially terminated.
